facts.statement: Crocodylus lucivenator is a new species of crocodile in the genus Crocodylus.
facts.quote: A crocodile, a species of Crocodylus.

facts.statement: It lived in the Late Pliocene in the Hadar Formation of Ethiopia.
facts.quote: from the Late Pliocene Hadar Formation of Ethiopia

facts.statement: The Hadar Formation lies in the Afar region of north-east Ethiopia.
facts.quote: located in Afar Regional State, north-east Ethiopia

facts.statement: Its holotype, A.L. 138-16, a full skull with the matching lower jaw, is the best-preserved specimen.
facts.quote: The holotype of Crocodylus lucivenator is specimen A.L. 138-16, a complete cranium with the matching lower jaw and the most complete specimen known.

facts.statement: Many more fossils were referred to the species, including skulls, isolated bones, teeth and osteoderms.
facts.quote: The referred material includes a number of well preserved skulls along with isolated cranial and postcranial remains, teeth and osteoderms.

facts.statement: Brochu and colleagues found no evidence of any other distinct crocodylian species at Hadar, unlike the Turkana Basin of Kenya.
facts.quote: Brochu and colleagues argue that there is no evidence for any other readily distinguishable crocodylian species from the sediments, unlike Pliocene fossil localities of the Turkana Basin in Kenya

facts.statement: Its name comes from Latin words meaning light and hunter.
facts.quote: derives from the Latin words "luci" and "venator" meaning "light" and "hunter" respectively

facts.statement: The name also alludes to Lucy, a famous Australopithecus afarensis fossil from the same formation.
facts.quote: it simultaneously alludes to Lucy, a famous specimen of the early hominid Australopithecus afarensis also known from the Hadar Formation

facts.statement: Nothing shows that a known specimen hunted Lucy herself, but the species likely preyed on Australopithecus.
facts.quote: While there is no evidence any of the known specimens hunted Lucy specifically, as a whole the species would have likely preyed on members of the genus Australopithecus.

facts.statement: A raised bump on the snout in front of the eyes, a rostral boss, helps characterize it.
facts.quote: is characterized in part by the presence of a rostral boss before the eyes

facts.statement: It seems closely related to the extinct paleoafrican Crocodylus of East Africa, not to Africa's living crocodiles.
facts.quote: appears to be closely related to paleoafrican Crocodylus species from East Africa rather than the crocodiles that inhabit the continent today

facts.statement: The largest individuals reached 4-5 m long and probably weighed 300-600 kg.
facts.quote: The largest specimens of Crocodylus lucivenator reached a length between 4-5 m and likely reached a weight between 300-600 kg.

facts.statement: Its tooth count matches its closest relatives: 13 to 14 teeth in each upper jaw bone and 15 to 16 in each lower jaw.
facts.quote: With five premaxillary teeth, 13 to 14 maxillary teeth and 15 to 16 teeth in the lower jaw, the tooth count of Crocodylus lucivenator matches that of its closest relatives.

facts.statement: Specimen A.L. 126-11 shows several injuries along its lower jaw.
facts.quote: Specimen A.L. 126-11 of Crocodylus lucivenator preserves several lesions along the dentary

facts.statement: Those wounds healed and were most likely caused by another crocodile.
facts.quote: suggests that the animal was injured by another crocodile

facts.statement: With its size and sturdy skull it is seen as a generalist ambush predator, probably the top predator of its environment.
facts.quote: Crocodylus lucivenator is interpreted to have been a macro-generalist ambush predator, likely the apex of its native environment

facts.statement: The Hadar Formation records a mix of woodland and grassland, with large lakes at times.
facts.quote: The Hadar Formation is described as preserving a mixed environment of woodlands and grasslands with large palaeolakes present during some points in time.

facts.statement: The naming study, titled Lucy's peril, appeared in 2026 in the Journal of Systematic Palaeontology.
facts.quote:
Journal: Journal of Systematic Palaeontology
Year: 2026

sentences.text: Crocodylus lucivenator was a crocodile whose largest individuals reached 4-5 m in length and probably weighed 300-600 kg.
One of its distinguishing features is a rostral boss, a raised bump on top of the snout just in front of the eyes.
Its tooth count matches that of its closest relatives, with 13 to 14 teeth in each upper jaw bone and 15 to 16 in each lower jaw.
The holotype, A.L. 138-16, a full skull with its matching lower jaw, is the best-preserved specimen, and many more skulls, bones, teeth and osteoderms have been assigned to the species.
Its name joins Latin words for light and hunter, and it also winks at Lucy, the famous Australopithecus afarensis fossil found in the same rocks.
Brochu and colleagues described it in 2026 in the Journal of Systematic Palaeontology, in a study titled Lucy's peril.
Large and with a sturdy skull, it is interpreted as a versatile ambush predator, probably at the top of its food chain.
Nothing shows that any known specimen attacked Lucy herself, but the species very likely hunted members of her genus, Australopithecus.
One specimen, A.L. 126-11, carries healed injuries on its lower jaw, most likely left by another crocodile.
It seems to belong to the extinct paleoafrican branch of Crocodylus from East Africa, rather than to the crocodiles living in Africa today.
It lived in the Late Pliocene, in the Hadar Formation of the Afar region of Ethiopia.
Its home mixed woodland and grassland, at times with large lakes, and it seems to have been the only crocodile there, unlike the Turkana Basin of Kenya.
Crocodylus lucivenator fue un cocodrilo cuyos ejemplares más grandes alcanzaban de 4 a 5 m de longitud y probablemente pesaban entre 300 y 600 kg.
Uno de sus rasgos distintivos es una protuberancia rostral, un abultamiento en lo alto del hocico justo delante de los ojos.
Su número de dientes coincide con el de sus parientes más cercanos: de 13 a 14 en cada maxilar y de 15 a 16 en cada mitad de la mandíbula.
El holotipo, A.L. 138-16, un cráneo completo con su mandíbula, es el ejemplar mejor conservado, y a la especie se le han atribuido muchos otros cráneos, huesos, dientes y osteodermos.
Su nombre une las palabras latinas para «luz» y «cazador», y además guiña a Lucy, el famoso fósil de Australopithecus afarensis hallado en las mismas rocas.
Brochu y sus colegas lo describieron en 2026 en el Journal of Systematic Palaeontology, en un estudio titulado «Lucy's peril» («El peligro de Lucy»).
Grande y con un cráneo robusto, se interpreta como un depredador de emboscada muy versátil, probablemente en la cima de su cadena alimentaria.
Nada indica que algún ejemplar conocido atacara a la propia Lucy, pero la especie muy probablemente cazaba miembros de su género, Australopithecus.
Un ejemplar, A.L. 126-11, presenta heridas ya curadas en la mandíbula, muy probablemente causadas por otro cocodrilo.
Parece pertenecer a la rama paleoafricana, hoy extinta, de Crocodylus del este de África, y no a los cocodrilos que viven hoy en el continente.
Vivió en el Plioceno Superior, en la Formación Hadar de la región de Afar, en Etiopía.
Su entorno combinaba bosques y praderas, a veces con grandes lagos, y parece haber sido el único cocodrilo del lugar, a diferencia de la cuenca del Turkana, en Kenia.
